title: A Morning of Street Food in Mexico City
paragraphs: Mexico City is famous for its street food, and the best way to discover it is on foot. Last Saturday I joined a tour with a local guide called Fernanda, who has been showing visitors her favourite stalls for six years. There were eight of us, and we started at nine in the morning.

Our first stop was a small stall that sold tamales, which are made with corn dough and filled with chicken, cheese or vegetables. They are wrapped in leaves and cooked with steam. A tamal cost twenty-five pesos, and a cup of hot atole cost fifteen. Fernanda told us that many people eat this breakfast on their way to work.

Next we walked to a market where a man was making tacos on a hot plate. The tacos were served with onion, coriander and a spicy green sauce. I am not very good with spicy food, so I asked for a mild one, but my friend Kenji, who loves chilli, put extra sauce on everything. His face turned red, and the whole group laughed.

Fernanda gave us some useful advice. She said that the best stalls are usually the ones with a queue, because that means the food is fresh and popular. She also recommended watching how the cook handles money and food, and bringing coins, since many stalls don't accept cards. Finally, she told us to drink bottled water, even if the juice looks delicious.

We finished with esquites, a warm cup of corn with mayonnaise, lime and chilli powder. I have never tasted anything like it. By noon I had tried six different dishes and spent less than two hundred pesos. I'm already planning to go back, and next time I will bring my cousins, who say they don't like Mexican food. I think I can change their minds.

title: Twenty-Four Hours to Build an Idea
focus: Past simple and past perfect in narrative
paragraphs: Nadia had never been to a hackathon, so she was nervous when she arrived at the university in Santiago on Friday afternoon. The event lasted twenty-four hours, and every team had to create an app that solved a problem in their city. Her team had three other members: Joaquín, Emre and Fiona. They had met only twenty minutes before.

At first they argued about the idea. Joaquín wanted to make a game, and Fiona preferred a map for tourists. Then Nadia remembered her grandmother, who finds it difficult to shop because the supermarket is far away and the stairs in her building are steep. 'What if neighbours could help each other?' she asked. Everyone stopped talking. They had found their idea.

The team divided the work. Emre, who was the best programmer, built the main screen. Fiona designed the logo and the colours, and Joaquín wrote the texts. Nadia tested the app with the other teams and asked them what they didn't understand. By three o'clock in the morning, the app crashed every time someone pressed the 'send' button, and they were all exhausted.

Nobody wanted to give up. Emre drank two cups of coffee, Fiona put on some quiet music, and Joaquín found the error: one tiny mistake in line two hundred. When the app finally worked at five o'clock, they shouted so loudly that a teacher came to see what had happened. Then they slept for an hour on the floor.

At noon on Saturday, each team had five minutes to present its project. Nadia was so nervous that her hands were shaking, but she remembered her grandmother and spoke clearly. They didn't win first prize because another team had built a robot. However, the judges gave them a special mention, and two neighbours from a local organisation asked to test the app. 'It was the best weekend of my year,' Nadia said afterwards.

title: My Grandmother's Blue Notebook
focus: Relative clauses with who, which and where
paragraphs: In my grandmother's kitchen in Cartagena there is a drawer that nobody is allowed to open. Inside it is a blue notebook with an old rubber band around it. She started writing in it when she was seventeen, and the pages, which are now yellow, still smell of coconut and cinnamon.

Last month, Grandma Nelly broke her wrist and could not cook for six weeks. 'Dayana, you are the only person who can save the family dinners,' she told me. I laughed because the only thing I had ever cooked was an omelette. But she gave me the notebook, and I accepted the challenge.

The first recipe I chose was arroz con coco, a dish that is very popular on the Caribbean coast of Colombia. I soon discovered that her instructions were not very precise. They said things like 'add a little salt' and 'cook until it smells right'. I called her five times in one hour, and each time she answered, 'You will know when it's ready.'

The rice was a disaster. It was too sweet, and some of it burned. But my brother Andrés, who is very honest, ate two plates. The next day I tried fried plantains, and they were better. By the end of the week I had cooked four of her recipes, and nobody in the family complained. Even Grandma, who is the strictest judge in the house, said, 'Not bad.'

Now I understand why she never wrote exact measurements. Cooking is not only about numbers. It is about tasting, smelling and learning from mistakes. I have also started adding my own notes in the margins, in green pen, so that the next person can follow the story. Perhaps one day my children will find this notebook, and they will know that three generations of women cooked in this house.

title: City Fights the Heat: A Hot Week in Buenos Aires
paragraphs: Buenos Aires has just finished its hottest week of the summer. According to the weather service, temperatures stayed above thirty-five degrees for six days, and the nights were hardly cooler. Many residents said that they couldn't sleep, and hospitals reported more patients than usual.

The city government opened twenty cooling centres in libraries and sports halls. 'Anyone can come in, rest and drink water,' said Marcela Ibarra, a city official. She added that older people and young children were the most at risk, and she asked neighbours to check on relatives who live alone.

Some businesses also changed their routines. A bakery in the neighbourhood of Caballito told customers that it would open at five in the morning and close at noon. The owner, Hugo Benítez, explained that the ovens made the kitchen unbearable in the afternoon. 'We lost some money,' he admitted, 'but my workers' health is more important.'

Schools were affected as well. A teacher at a secondary school said that her students had been falling asleep in class because of the heat. The headteacher decided that lessons would finish at one o'clock until the weather improved. Parents welcomed the decision, although some of them said that they had to change their work schedules.

Experts warn that heatwaves like this one may become more frequent. A university researcher, Dr Amina Torres, said that cities need more trees and shade, because green areas can be several degrees cooler than streets full of concrete. Meanwhile, the forecast says that temperatures will drop by the weekend, and people can finally open their windows at night.
glossary: ir a ver cómo está, controlar

title: What to Do If Someone Faints
paragraphs: Last Thursday my class took a first-aid course at school. The instructor, Mr Okafor, is a paramedic, and he started with a question: 'What would you do if a classmate fainted in front of you?' Most of us said, 'I would shout and run away.' He smiled and explained that the right reaction is much calmer.

First, you should stay calm and check that the area is safe. Then you must check whether the person is breathing. If they are not breathing, you have to call the emergency services immediately. If they are breathing, lay them on their back. You shouldn't try to sit them up, because their head needs to stay level with their body.

Next, raise their legs gently, about thirty centimetres above the floor. This helps the blood return to the brain. You should also loosen any tight clothes, for example a tie or a belt, and make sure that there is fresh air. Ask other people to move back so the person has space. You don't need to throw water on their face.

Most people wake up after a minute or two. When this happens, they mustn't stand up quickly. They should stay lying down for a few minutes and then sit up slowly. You can offer a drink of water, but only when they are fully awake. If the person doesn't recover after one minute, call the emergency services. You must also call for help if they have hit their head when falling.

At the end of the course, we practised with a partner. My friend Rania played the patient, and I had to follow the steps in order. I forgot to loosen her collar, so Mr Okafor reminded me. Now I feel more confident. He says everyone should take a course like this, because you never know when you might need it. I agree with him.

title: Seventeen and in Charge of the Game
focus: Present perfect and past simple in questions and answers
paragraphs: Ailín Suárez is seventeen years old and has already refereed more than sixty football matches in Montevideo. We met her after a Sunday morning game between two youth teams and asked her about this unusual hobby.
Q: Why did you decide to become a referee?

A: When I was fourteen, I played in my school team, and I was always arguing with the referee. One day the coach told me, 'If you think it's easy, try it.' So I took a course at the local football association. It lasted three months, and I was the only girl in the group.
Q: What is the hardest part of the job?

A: Definitely the parents. Some of them shout at me from the side of the pitch, even though the players are only twelve years old. At the beginning I felt terrible, and I almost quit after my third match. Now I just breathe and keep my attention on the game. I have learnt that you can't please everybody.
Q: Have you ever made a big mistake?

A: Yes, once. I gave a penalty that wasn't a penalty, and the team that lost was very angry. After the match I watched the video and saw my error. The next week, I apologised to the coach. He said that he respected me more because I admitted it.
Q: What would you say to other teenagers who want to try?

A: Be prepared to run a lot, and be ready to hear criticism. But you will also learn to make quick decisions and to stay calm under pressure. Those skills will help you in any job. And you will see the best part of every match: the handshake at the end when everybody has forgotten the arguments.

title: Three Days in Lisbon on a Student Budget
paragraphs: Lisbon is a city for people who love views, and the good news is that most of the views are free. I spent three days there last spring with my friend Carlos, and we spent less than two hundred euros each, including the hostel.

We stayed in a hostel in the old neighbourhood of Alfama, where a bed in a shared room cost around twenty euros a night. Breakfast was included, so we ate a lot of bread, cheese and fruit before leaving. The hostel also organised a free walking tour on the first evening, which was a good way to meet other travellers.

Lisbon is built on hills, so you should wear comfortable shoes. The streets are steeper than in many other cities, and the pavements can be slippery when it rains. If you get tired, you can take one of the old yellow trams, but be careful: the most famous line is always full, and pickpockets are common.

Food was cheaper than we expected. The best thing we ate was a pastel de nata, a small custard tart, which cost less than two euros in a local bakery. Carlos ate at least seven during our stay. For lunch, many restaurants offer a 'dish of the day' that is much cheaper than the menu, and the portions are big enough to share.

If I had to choose one thing to recommend, I would say: climb to a viewpoint at sunset. Take a bottle of water, some snacks and a jacket, because the wind can be cold. We sat on a wall with two strangers who became friends, and we watched the sky turn orange over the river. It didn't cost anything, and it was my favourite moment of the trip.

title: Students Build a Drone to Find Lost Hikers
focus: Passive voice (past simple and present perfect)
paragraphs: A team of students from a technical school in San José, Costa Rica, has built a drone that can help rescue workers find missing hikers. The project was started last year by Joselyn Araya, who is eighteen, after a tourist was lost for two days in the mountains near her village.

The drone is equipped with a thermal camera, which shows the heat of living bodies. In daylight, a person can be seen from far away, but at night it is much more difficult. With the thermal camera, a hiker can be located even in the dark. The images are sent to a tablet that is held by the rescue team.

The students built the first version in a school workshop, using parts that were donated by local companies. It was tested many times in a field near the school, and several problems were found. The battery, for example, lasted only ten minutes, so a new one had to be ordered. Their teacher, Daniel Kim, says that the mistakes were the most valuable part of the project.

Last month the drone was used for the first time in a real search. A group of three teenagers who had left the path were found in less than an hour. They were cold and tired, but none of them was injured. 'Everyone in the control tent shouted when we saw them on the screen,' says Joselyn.

The team now wants to improve the drone so that it can fly in strong wind. They also hope that other schools will copy the idea, and the plans have been published online for free. However, Joselyn is realistic. 'A drone can't replace a trained rescuer,' she says. 'It's just one more tool to make the search faster and safer.'

title: A Few Ideas for Our Flat
focus: Suggestions: should, could, why don't we, how about
paragraphs: Hi all,

I hope you are having a good week. I'd like to talk about some small problems in our flat in Madrid before they become big ones. Please don't think I'm angry. I just believe that a few simple rules would make our life easier.

First, the dishes. Yesterday there were nine plates in the sink, and some of them had been there for three days. I suggest that everyone washes their dishes immediately after eating. If you are in a hurry, please put them in water so that the food doesn't dry.

Second, the cleaning. At the moment we don't have a system, so I always end up doing the bathroom. How about a weekly rota? Each of us would clean a different area every Saturday: the kitchen, the bathroom, the living room and the hall. We could change areas every week so nobody gets stuck with the worst job.

Third, the bills. Hamza is paying the internet bill every month and then asking for the money, which isn't fair. Why don't we open a shared account? If we each put in twenty euros a month, we will always have enough for electricity, water and internet. We can check the numbers together on the first day of each month.

Finally, visitors. I love having friends over, but I think we should tell each other in advance if someone is staying the night. Nobody should feel uncomfortable in their own home. Let's meet on Sunday evening at eight to discuss these ideas. I will bring some snacks! If you can't come, send me a message and tell me what you think.
Ingrid

title: The Poems on the Back of Bus Tickets
paragraphs: Wara had been writing poems since she was ten, but she had never shown them to anyone. She was too shy. In La Paz, where she lived with her aunt, she travelled every day by minibus to her school, and during the journey she wrote small poems on the back of the used tickets that she found on the floor.

One morning she did something strange. When she got off the minibus, she left a poem on her seat. It said: 'The city is a mountain of voices, and today I am listening.' She didn't sign it. She walked to school feeling embarrassed and excited at the same time.

After that, she left a poem every week, always in a different minibus. Sometimes she imagined who would find them: a tired nurse, a schoolboy, an old man with a hat. She never found out. Then, one Friday, the driver of her usual minibus, Don Rubén, turned on the radio, and Wara heard her own words.

'Listeners,' said the presenter, 'a driver sent me this poem last week. Nobody knows who wrote it. If you are the author, please call us.' Wara's heart began to beat very fast. She looked around, but nobody in the minibus had noticed anything. She had been afraid that people would laugh at her poems, and now a stranger was reading one on the radio.

That afternoon she called the station. The presenter invited her to read a poem on the programme the following Sunday. Wara was terrified, but she accepted. Don Rubén told her that he had collected twelve of her tickets in a small box. 'I knew they were yours,' he said with a smile. 'Nobody else writes so neatly.' Now Wara still writes on tickets, but she signs them.
